See also: Frigo, frigó, and frigo-

Dutch

[edit]

Etymology

[edit]

Borrowed from French frigo, apocopic form of réfrigérateur.

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • IPA(key): /ˈfriɣoː/
  • Audio:(file)

Noun

[edit]

frigo m (plural frigo's, diminutive frigootje n)

  1. (Belgium) fridge, refrigerator

Synonyms

[edit]
  • (fridge): ijskast, koelkast

French

[edit]

Etymology

[edit]

Clipping of frigorifique, frigorifié, or réfrigérateur.

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • IPA(key): /fʁi.ɡo/

Noun

[edit]

frigo m (plural frigos)

  1. (colloquial) fridge; refrigerator

Coordinate terms

[edit]
  • congélateur
  • frigidaire
  • réfrigérateur

Descendants

[edit]
  • → Dutch: frigo
  • → Norman: frigo

Further reading

[edit]
  • “frigo”, in Trésor de la langue française informatisé [Digitized Treasury of the French Language], 2012

Italian

[edit]

Etymology

[edit]

Clipping of frigorifero.

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • IPA(key): /ˈfri.ɡo/
  • Rhymes: -iɡo
  • Hyphenation: frì‧go
  • Audio:(file)

Noun

[edit]

frigo m (invariable)

  1. fridge, refrigerator
    Synonym: frigorifero

Anagrams

[edit]
  • Grifo, forgi, grifo, grofi

Latin

[edit]

Etymology

[edit]

Possibly from a Proto-Indo-European *bʰer(H)-g- (“to roast, grill, fry”); cf. Ancient Greek φρύγω (phrúgō, “to roast, bake”), Sanskrit भृज्जति (bhṛjjati, “to roast, grill, fry”), भृग् (bhṛg, “the crackling of fire”). However, Latin frīg- would point to *bʰreyg⁽ʰ⁾-, which lacks formal cognates. De Vaan suggests the word is a loan from late Ancient Greek or another source, following Giacomelli (1994), who assumes it is a late Greek borrowing. Probably related to Umbrian frehtu.[1] See also fertum.

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • (Classical Latin) IPA(key): [ˈfriː.ɡoː]
  • (modern Italianate Ecclesiastical) IPA(key): [ˈfriː.ɡo]

Verb

[edit]

frīgō (present infinitive frīgere, perfect active frīxī, supine frīctum or frīxum); third conjugation

  1. to roast, fry
  2. to parch
    • 1934, Cato, Varro, Agriculture, Harvard University Press, page 98:
      Sesquilibram salis frigito, eodem indito et rude misceto usque adeo, donec ovum gallinaceum coctum natabit, desinito miscere.
      Parch half a pound of salt, add it in, and stir with a stick, until a boiled chicken egg floats, then stop stiring.
